data.title: On-Site Impersonation of Staff and Contractors
data.summary: A pretext as a contractor, auditor or internal IT staff member was accepted without verification, obtaining escorted and then unescorted access to restricted areas and to equipment, including assistance from staff in reaching it.
data.description:
Impersonation on site combines the physical and psychological dimensions: the attacker is present, which lends credibility that no email can, and presents a role that staff are conditioned not to obstruct.

Maintenance and IT pretexts are effective because they are both unremarkable and unwelcome to question — the visitor is doing something tedious on someone else's behalf, and challenging them risks delaying work. A high-visibility vest, a clipboard, a laptop and a plausible job reference are usually enough.

The most valuable outcome is assistance rather than access: staff who unlock the comms room, log the visitor into a system "to test it", or explain which cabinet holds what. These are helpful acts by people doing their jobs, which is why instruction alone rarely changes them.
data.recommendation:
* Verify all contractor and maintenance visits against a work order raised in advance by a named internal owner, confirmed by telephone before access.
* Make role claims verifiable: publish the way IT identifies itself, and state clearly that IT will never ask a user to log in on their behalf or to hand over a device without a ticket.
* Require escort for all external parties in technical areas, with the escort named and present throughout.
* Give staff a no-blame route to check a visitor — a single number to call — so verification does not require confrontation.
* Record and review the identity verification actually performed, not just the visit.
data.short_recommendation: Verify contractors against a work order before granting access.
